nameStory: Swamp candles gets its charming name from its tall spikes of bright yellow flowers that rise up like flickering candles from wetland areas. The flowers bloom from bottom to top along the spike, creating the illusion of a candle being lit gradually upward. Its other common name, lake loosestrife, refers to its preferred watery habitat and its membership in the loosestrife group.
description: Swamp candles is a native perennial wildflower that grows 1-4 feet tall in wet areas throughout New England. It produces distinctive tall, narrow spikes of small bright yellow flowers that bloom from late spring through summer. The plant has simple, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately along sturdy upright stems. Despite its delicate-looking flowers, this is a robust wetland plant that often forms colonies in marshy areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers arranged in a tall, narrow spike or raceme, blooming progressively from bottom to top. Each small flower has 5 pointed petals and feels papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves 2-6 inches long, arranged alternately up the stem (not in pairs). Leaves feel smooth and slightly waxy, with prominent parallel veins visible when held up to light.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in upright clumps 1-4 feet tall with multiple stems arising from the base. Stems are sturdy, smooth, and often reddish-tinged, especially near the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round capsules develop after flowering, starting green and turning brown. When ripe, they split open to release tiny seeds that feel like fine sand between your fingers.

habitat: Swamp candles thrives in consistently moist to wet soils in marshes, swamps, pond edges, wet meadows, and roadside ditches. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, blue flag iris, and other wetland plants in areas that stay soggy most of the year. It tolerates both full sun and partial shade but needs that constant moisture to flourish.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as reddish stems with unfurling leaves. Flower spikes begin forming in late spring, appearing as tight green buds at stem tips.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with brilliant yellow flower spikes at their showiest from June through August. This is the best time for identification when the candle-like flower spikes are unmistakable.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules ripen to brown. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, and dried flower stalks persist with opened seed capsules.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots. Only dried brown stems and old flower stalks may remain visible above ground in protected areas.

funFact: Swamp candles flowers contain natural soap-like compounds called saponins - you can actually create a light lather by crushing the petals with water between your hands, though it won't smell particularly pleasant!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with goldenrod, but swamp candles has flowers in a single narrow spike while goldenrod has branching, more feathery flower clusters. Remember: 'Candles are straight and narrow, goldenrod spreads and branches.' Also, swamp candles grows only in wet areas while most goldenrods prefer drier soils.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'lake loosestrife,' this native plant is completely different from the invasive purple loosestrife that chokes out wetlands. The name 'loosestrife' comes from an old belief that these plants could calm angry oxen - though swamp candles is much more peaceful in the ecosystem than its purple namesake!
compareHints: Among its loosestrife relatives, swamp candles is unique for its tall, narrow flower spike - most other Lysimachia species have flowers in leaf axils or shorter, broader clusters. Whorled loosestrife has flowers in circles around the stem, while fringed loosestrife has broader, more scattered flowers. Yellow loosestrife has similar colored flowers but grows in more branching, rounded clusters rather than the distinctive candle-like spike.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its loosestrife relatives that tend to be taller with yellow flowers and different leaf arrangements, northern starflower is much shorter with its distinctive white seven-petaled blooms and single whorl of leaves.
Among New England's many Lysimachia species, whorled loosestrife is instantly recognizable by its four-leaf whorls - no other loosestrife has this arrangement.
Among New England's loosestrifes, fringed loosestrife is distinctive for its opposite leaves with fringed leaf stems and nodding yellow flowers.
Among its loosestrife relatives in New England, creeping Jenny is unique for its trailing, mat-forming habit - most other Lysimachia species stand upright.
Dotted loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife cousins mainly by those telltale petal spots - no other Lysimachia species has them.
Unlike its loosestrife cousins in the same genus, scarlet pimpernel stays ground-hugging rather than growing upright, and its flowers are much smaller but more intensely colored.
Among the loosestrife family in New England, gooseneck loosestrife is the only one with the distinctive curved white flower spikes.
Unlike its loosestrife relatives that are mostly freshwater plants with showy yellow or white flowers, sea milkwort is the oddball of the family - adapted for salt water and lacking petals entirely.

Yellow loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife relatives by its tall stature and dense yellow flower clusters - most other Lysimachia species in New England are shorter with more scattered flowers.
Among its loosestrife cousins, tufted loosestrife is unique for having flowers that emerge from the sides of the stem rather than at the tips.

Among New England's yellow-flowered loosestrifes, lowland loosestrife is distinguished by its flowers tucked into leaf axils rather than arranged in showy spikes like swamp candles, or whorled around the stem like whorled loosestrife.
Among its loosestrife relatives, lanceleaf loosestrife is distinguished by its alternate (not opposite or whorled) leaf arrangement and narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Unlike its flashy cousin creeping Jenny (regular moneywort), miniature moneywort is truly miniature in every way - much smaller leaves, tinier flowers, and more delicate growth.

Unlike other Lysimachia species in New England that tend to be taller perennials with yellow flowers (like whorled loosestrife or swamp candles), blue scarlet pimpernel is a tiny blue-flowered annual that creeps along the ground.
